hits.name: John Crickett
hits.text:
“AI will replace software engineers because it can write all the code.”

Nope.

Several years ago I built software that unlocked more than $10M a year in additional profit for the business.

The code took less than two weeks.

With today’s AI tools, I could probably do it in under a week. Maybe even a day.

But the code wasn’t the hard part.

The hard part took months:

Understanding a messy domain.

Pressure-testing assumptions with experts.

Working through edge cases.

Deciding what not to build.

Making tradeoffs around risk, complexity, and value, then getting stakeholders to sign off on them.

By the time I wrote most of the code, much of the real engineering had already happened.

That’s why “AI can write code, therefore AI can replace engineers” misses the point.

Code is an output of engineering.

AI makes that output faster and cheaper.

But someone still has to understand the problem, challenge the assumptions, make the tradeoffs, and decide what the software should actually do.

That’s the engineering.

hits.name: Akshay 🚀
hits.text:
Big win for AI Engineers!

If you're deploying agents in production, this one is for you.

(bookmark it)

There's a new system that can test and evaluate your agents against the real world, then write the fixes, all before you deploy them.

AI agents look great in demos, until real users start breaking them. Your agent can tell a customer "refund done" on a $1,080 invoice without ever checking who she is, and the logs will still look clean.

Normally you only find a failure like that after a real customer runs into it. @pluraiAI Simulation lets your agent fail in a simulated world first, so you can fix the problem before any user sees it.

↳ It rebuilds your actual agent, its tools and its environment from your code

↳ Simulated users push the agent into the edge cases that matter for your use case

↳ Evals built for your agent check the actions it took, like whether it verified the customer before issuing that refund

↳ Every failure comes with the run that exposed it and a fix you can verify

↳ Any production failure can become a simulation you replay against every new version

It ships as a single plugin for coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, and it works with whatever agent you're building. I've started running it on my own agents too.

It's free for every AI engineer. Link in the first comment.

I worked with the Plurai team to put this together. Here's the whole system, step by step, from the first simulated user to a re-tested fix:
